questions.stem: A benefits coordinator built a Project that answers staff questions using the uploaded 2026 Benefits Guide. Its instructions set the role, audience and tone. When an employee asked about adoption support, which the guide does not mention, Claude gave a confident answer with a specific reimbursement amount that does not exist. Which change to the project instructions would MOST directly prevent this kind of answer?

options.text: Add the line 'Always be accurate and double-check every figure before you answer an employee.'
Tell Claude it is a senior benefits expert with deep knowledge of typical company benefit plans.
Tell Claude that if the guide doesn't cover a question, it should say so and point the employee to the benefits inbox.
Ask Claude to end every answer with a confidence score from 1 to 10 so employees can judge it.

questions.explanation: The instructions had no rule for **missing information**, so Claude filled the gap with something plausible. Anthropic's guidance on reducing hallucinations recommends explicitly allowing Claude to say it doesn't know and restricting answers to the provided documents. A concrete fallback (say it isn't covered, send people to the benefits inbox) gives Claude a safe action to take instead of guessing.

whyWrong.A: 'Be accurate' is a vague quality word with no action attached. It doesn't tell Claude what to do when the guide is silent, which is exactly where the error happened.
whyWrong.B: Calling Claude an expert in 'typical' plans makes the problem worse: it invites answers drawn from general knowledge rather than from this company's actual guide.
whyWrong.D: A self-rated confidence score is not a reliable signal and still lets the invented amount reach the employee. It adds noise without fixing the missing rule.

questions.mindset: Every instruction set needs a rule for what to do when the sources don't have the answer.

questions.stem: A fundraising manager set her account-wide instructions months ago to say 'Always format answers as short bullet points.' She has now created a Project for drafting personal thank-you letters to major donors, with project instructions asking for warm, flowing letters. Some letters come out as prose and others as bullet lists, even for similar requests. With the LEAST disruption to her other work, what should she do?

options.text: Scope the account-wide rule (for example, 'use bullets for my notes and summaries') so it no longer clashes with letter-writing.
Add 'IMPORTANT: ignore any formatting instructions from anywhere else' in capital letters to the project instructions.
Delete all of her account-wide instructions so that only project instructions ever shape Claude's responses.
Regenerate each letter until it comes out in prose, since the inconsistency is random and will not follow a pattern.

questions.explanation: Account-wide instructions apply to **all** chats, and project instructions add context for one body of work. Here the two layers contradict each other, so the output flips between them. The fix is to remove the conflict at its source: narrow the account-wide rule so it is true everywhere it applies. Her bullet-point preference keeps working for notes, and the donor project gets clean prose.

whyWrong.B: Shouting an override leaves the conflict in place and makes outputs depend on which instruction wins on a given day. It is also a blunt rule that may suppress formatting she does want, such as a list of enclosed items.
whyWrong.C: Deleting every account-wide preference throws away settings that help all her other chats. That is far more disruption than needed to fix one conflicting line.
whyWrong.D: The inconsistency has a clear cause: two instructions pulling in opposite directions. Regenerating treats the symptom and costs time on every letter.

questions.mindset: When outputs flip between styles, look for contradictory instructions across layers and fix the conflict, not the symptom.

questions.stem: A customer service team's Project instructions include the rule 'Never mention delivery dates.' Claude now refuses even to tell customers that the warehouse will email them a tracking link, and some replies sound evasive. The team lead wants Claude to handle delivery questions sensibly, including cases nobody wrote a rule for. Which rewrite is MOST likely to achieve that?

options.text: List the twenty most common delivery questions in the instructions with an approved answer written out for each one.
Change the rule to 'NEVER, under any circumstances, mention delivery dates or anything at all about deliveries.'
Remove the rule entirely and trust Claude to use good judgment about what to say when customers ask about deliveries.
Explain the reason — dates come from the courier and often change — and describe the tracking process customers can rely on instead.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's prompting guidance notes that giving the **context or motivation** behind an instruction helps Claude understand the goal and respond in a more targeted way. Once Claude knows *why* dates are off-limits (they're unreliable and owned by the courier), it can still be helpful about the parts that are safe, like the tracking email, and apply the same logic to questions nobody anticipated. A bare prohibition gets applied too literally.

whyWrong.A: A long list of scripted answers only covers the cases someone predicted and bloats the instructions. The lead explicitly wants good handling of unforeseen questions.
whyWrong.B: Making the prohibition broader and louder makes the evasive behavior worse. Claude would now avoid even the helpful tracking information.
whyWrong.C: Removing the rule brings back the original risk of Claude promising specific dates that the courier may not meet.

questions.mindset: Give the reason behind a rule so Claude can apply its intent, not just its wording.

questions.stem: A city council communications officer set up a Project for public notices. Its instructions say 'Don't use jargon. Don't write long sentences. Don't be too formal.' Notices still contain terms like 'remediation works' and residents complain they are hard to read. What is the BEST way to strengthen these instructions?

options.text: Add more prohibitions, such as 'Don't use technical words, acronyms, legal terms or anything residents won't know.'
State what to do: write for the general public in sentences under about 20 words, and explain any technical term in everyday words.
Ask Claude to rate how readable each notice is on a scale of 1 to 10 and rewrite any notice that scores below 8.
Upload a full dictionary of plain-English alternatives as project knowledge and say to consult it when needed.

questions.explanation: Claude's prompting guidance recommends telling Claude **what to do instead of what not to do**. A list of 'don'ts' leaves the target undefined. Naming the audience (the general public), a concrete sentence-length target and a clear behavior for unavoidable technical terms gives Claude something specific and checkable to aim for.

whyWrong.A: More negatives still don't describe the desired writing. Claude has to guess what counts as 'technical', which is how 'remediation works' slipped through.
whyWrong.C: A self-assigned readability score is not a dependable measure, and it adds a step without telling Claude who the readers are or what plain writing looks like.
whyWrong.D: A large reference file adds bulk without fixing the instruction itself. The problem is an undefined target, not a missing vocabulary list.

questions.mindset: Describe the target behavior positively and specifically; a list of don'ts leaves Claude guessing.

questions.stem: An executive assistant created a 'Board Support' Project in March. Its instructions read: 'You support the CEO's office. Summarise the March board pack in one page, focusing on the financial results. Use formal UK English.' In April she starts a new chat in the project to draft a thank-you note to a retiring director, and Claude's reply keeps bringing up March financial results. What is the MOST appropriate fix?

options.text: Add a line saying 'Ignore anything about March unless I ask about it' at the top of the existing instructions.
Create a separate new Project for each month so that last month's instructions never affect this month's chats.
Keep the standing role and style rules in the instructions, and move the one-off March summary request into a chat.
Switch to a more capable model that is better at working out which parts of the instructions apply to the task.

questions.explanation: Project instructions apply to **every** chat in the project, so they should hold only what is always true: role, audience, style, standing rules. 'Summarise the March board pack' is a one-time **task request** that belongs in a message. Leaving it in the instructions makes Claude treat it as relevant to every chat, which is why March results keep appearing.

whyWrong.A: Adding a patch line around a task that shouldn't be in the instructions keeps the clutter and invites new contradictions. The fix is to move the task out.
whyWrong.B: A new project every month duplicates setup and knowledge for no reason. The real problem is one misplaced line, not the project itself.
whyWrong.D: Claude is doing what the instructions say. A different model can't fix instructions that state a one-off task as if it were a standing rule.

questions.mindset: Standing instructions hold what is always true; one-off requests belong in the chat.

questions.stem: Over a year, several team members have added lines to a shared proposal-writing Project's instructions. They now run to four pages and include the full company history, product descriptions copied from the brochure, and rules that nobody remembers adding. Claude increasingly misses the two rules that matter most: the required section order and the ban on quoting prices. Which approach would MOST effectively restore reliable behavior?

options.text: Cut the instructions to the essential rules, move reference material into project knowledge, then test with real requests.
Move the two key rules to the very top and mark them 'CRITICAL', leaving the rest of the four pages unchanged.
Copy the two key rules into every new chat as well, so Claude sees them twice: once in instructions and once in the message.
Split the instructions across three Projects so each one has a shorter set of instructions to follow.

questions.explanation: Every line in standing instructions competes for attention, and reference content (company history, product copy) is **knowledge**, not instruction. Pruning to the rules that actually change the output, moving background material to project knowledge where Claude can draw on it when needed, and then testing with real requests addresses the root cause: bloat and noise burying the rules that matter.

whyWrong.B: Emphasis doesn't remove the clutter or the old rules nobody remembers, some of which may conflict with the key ones. The two rules would still compete with four pages of noise.
whyWrong.C: Pasting rules into every chat is the manual repetition a Project is meant to remove, and people will forget. It works around the problem instead of fixing the instructions.
whyWrong.D: Splitting one body of work across three Projects fragments knowledge and creates three sets of instructions to keep in sync, without removing the clutter.

questions.mindset: Short, essential instructions beat long ones; background belongs in knowledge, not in the rules.

questions.stem: A compliance analyst wrote this in a team Project's instructions: 'CRITICAL: You MUST ALWAYS add the full regulatory disclaimer to EVERY response.' The disclaimer is only required on material that goes to clients. Colleagues now get a long disclaimer appended to quick internal answers, such as which meeting room to book. What is the BEST correction?

options.text: Keep the rule as written and ask colleagues to delete the disclaimer by hand whenever it isn't needed.
Remove the disclaimer rule entirely and rely on colleagues to remember to add it to client material.
Add a second rule in capitals: 'NEVER add the disclaimer to internal messages', alongside the first rule.
Rewrite it with the condition and the reason: add the disclaimer to drafts meant for clients, because regulators require it.

questions.explanation: The rule fails because it is **absolute and unconditional**: written as 'EVERY response', it gives Claude no way to distinguish client-facing material from a quick internal question, so it gets applied everywhere. Rewriting it with the condition (drafts going to clients) and the reason (regulators require it) follows Anthropic's guidance to give the motivation behind a rule, which helps Claude apply its intent rather than just its wording.

whyWrong.A: Leaving a known-bad rule in place pushes repetitive cleanup onto every colleague and trains people to ignore output they should be reading.
whyWrong.B: The disclaimer is a regulatory requirement for client material. Removing the rule swaps an annoyance for a compliance risk.
whyWrong.C: Two shouted absolutes that pull against each other create a conflict Claude has to resolve on every response. One clear conditional rule is simpler and more reliable.

questions.mindset: State the condition and the reason for a rule; unconditional absolutes get applied to everything.

questions.stem: A research team's Project instructions say 'Be thorough and cover every relevant detail' and, a few lines later, 'Keep responses concise.' Some answers are a few lines and others run to several pages for similar questions, and the team can't predict which they will get. What should the project owner change to get consistent results?

options.text: Delete 'Keep responses concise' so that Claude always gives the most complete answer it can produce.
Resolve the tension with a clear rule, such as a short summary first and full detail only when the user asks for it.
Add 'Use your best judgment to balance thoroughness and brevity' as a third line beneath the other two.
Ask team members to say 'short' or 'long' at the start of each message so Claude knows which line to follow.

questions.explanation: 'Thorough' and 'concise' pull in opposite directions with no tie-breaker, so Claude resolves the conflict differently each time. Replacing them with a single, specific rule (for example, a short summary up front, with detail on request) removes the contradiction and gives the team predictable output. Anthropic's guidance on consistency stresses clear, precise instructions about the desired output format.

whyWrong.A: Removing one side fixes the inconsistency but swings every answer to maximum length, which is unlikely to be what a busy research team needs.
whyWrong.C: Asking Claude to 'balance' the two restates the conflict without defining the target. Results will stay unpredictable.
whyWrong.D: Pushing the decision onto every user in every message undoes the point of standing instructions and depends on everyone remembering.

questions.mindset: Contradictory instructions need a tie-breaker; vague 'balance' wording just restates the conflict.

questions.stem: A school administrator uses a Project to turn rough staff-meeting notes into minutes. The instructions describe the format in a long paragraph, but the layout of the minutes still varies from week to week: headings move around and action items are sometimes buried in the text. What is the MOST efficient way to make the format consistent?

options.text: Rewrite the paragraph describing the format so it is twice as long and covers every possible variation.
Upload all of last year's minutes as knowledge so Claude can work out the usual format from them.
Add one short sample of the desired minutes layout to the instructions, clearly marked as an example of the format.
Ask Claude at the end of each chat whether the minutes follow the format, and fix them if it says no.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's guidance calls examples one of the most reliable ways to steer **format, tone and structure**, and more effective than abstract instructions. A single short, clearly labeled sample of the layout (headings in order, action items in their own section) shows Claude exactly what 'right' looks like, which a long description often fails to do.

whyWrong.A: A longer description adds more words for Claude to interpret and more room for ambiguity. A concrete example is clearer.
whyWrong.B: A year of past minutes probably contains the same inconsistencies, so Claude may copy the variation. It also loads lots of material just to convey one layout.
whyWrong.D: Claude's own yes/no check is not a reliable control, and it adds a manual step to every meeting instead of fixing the instructions.

questions.mindset: Show, don't just tell: one clear example of the format often beats a paragraph describing it.

questions.stem: A quality team uses a Project to summarize customer complaints into a weekly report that is shared with an outside service vendor. Company policy says the report must not contain customers' personal data. The current instruction just says 'Be careful with private information.' The team wants the MOST reliable setup with reasonable effort. Which TWO actions should they take? Choose TWO.

options.text: Add 'This is EXTREMELY IMPORTANT' in capitals before the existing instruction so Claude gives it more weight.
Make the instruction specific: list what counts as personal data and say to replace it with a neutral label.
Ask Claude to finish each report with a statement confirming that it contains no personal data at all.
Switch the Project to the most capable model, since it will be better at recognizing private details.
Keep a named person responsible for checking each report for personal data before it goes to the vendor.

questions.explanation: 'Be careful' gives Claude nothing concrete to act on. A specific instruction (names, emails, phone numbers, account numbers, addresses, replaced with a label such as 'Customer A') makes the right behavior far more likely. But instructions are **guidance, not guarantees**, and this report leaves the company and involves personal data under a policy. A named human check before sending is the control that actually enforces the policy.

whyWrong.A: Louder wording doesn't define what 'private information' means, so Claude still has to guess. Emphasis is not a control.
whyWrong.C: A self-written 'no personal data' statement is not verification. If Claude missed something, it can just as easily miss it in its own confirmation.
whyWrong.D: Any model works better with a clear definition, and no model choice removes the need for a check when policy and an outside party are involved.

questions.mindset: Write precise instructions, and pair them with human review wherever policy or external exposure is at stake.

questions.stem: An independent consultant uses Claude daily. She has a separate Project for each client. She wants to set up the following preferences. Which TWO belong in her account-wide instructions rather than in any single Project's instructions? Choose TWO.

options.text: 'I'm an independent change-management consultant, and I mostly work with mid-sized healthcare providers.'
'Refer to Northfield Clinic's staff as "colleagues" and its patients as "service users" in all drafts.'
'Base recommendations only on the interview notes and survey results uploaded to this project.'
'Use UK spelling and keep answers direct; skip long introductions before getting to the point.'
'Every deliverable for this client must use their six-part report template and their logo colors.'

questions.explanation: Account-wide instructions apply to **all** conversations, so they should hold things that are true everywhere: who she is, the kind of work she does, and her general communication preferences. Client-specific terminology, sources and templates are true only for one client's work, so they belong in that client's Project instructions. A useful rule: put each instruction at the narrowest layer where it is always true.

whyWrong.B: Northfield Clinic's terminology applies only to that client. Account-wide, it would leak into drafts for every other client.
whyWrong.C: 'Only use the files uploaded to this project' is tied to one Project's knowledge. Account-wide, it would make no sense in ordinary chats or other clients' projects.
whyWrong.E: One client's report template and brand colors are client-specific rules. They belong in that client's Project, not in instructions that shape every chat.

questions.mindset: Put each instruction at the narrowest layer where it is always true.

questions.stem: A sales manager set up a shared Project for her team to draft first emails to prospective customers. The only instruction is 'Be helpful.' Emails vary wildly in length and tone from rep to rep, and twice Claude suggested a discount that the company doesn't offer. Which TWO additions to the project instructions would MOST improve the emails? Choose TWO.

options.text: 'You are the world's most successful salesperson and you write the most persuasive emails ever written.'
'Always be accurate, professional and correct, and make sure you never make any mistakes in an email.'
'Emails go to operations directors at logistics firms: under 120 words, plain and friendly, ending with one clear next step.'
'After writing each email, give it a score from 1 to 10 for persuasiveness and rewrite it if the score is low.'
Upload the current price sheet as project knowledge and add: 'Mention only pricing and offers listed there; for anything else, tell the rep to check with sales ops.'

questions.explanation: The two problems are **inconsistent style** and **invented offers**. Defining the audience, length, tone and structure (C) gives every rep's emails the same target. Tying pricing to an approved uploaded source and giving Claude a fallback when the source is silent (E) closes the gap that produced the made-up discount. Both lines are specific and checkable.

whyWrong.A: Flattering role language adds no information about the audience, length or limits, and 'most persuasive ever' could even encourage overpromising.
whyWrong.B: Vague quality words such as 'accurate' and 'never make mistakes' give Claude nothing to act on and don't say where pricing should come from.
whyWrong.D: Self-scoring adds a step but no new information about the audience or pricing limits, and a self-rating is not a reliable quality check.

questions.mindset: Effective instructions name the audience and format, and tie risky facts to an approved source with a fallback.

questions.stem: A training coordinator has rewritten the instructions for a Project that answers new hires' onboarding questions. Before sharing the Project with 40 new starters next week, she wants confidence that the new instructions behave as intended. Which TWO steps are the MOST useful? Choose TWO.

options.text: Ask Claude in a chat whether it thinks the new instructions are clear, and accept its view if it says they are fine.
Run a small set of realistic questions she already knows the answers to and check each reply against the rules.
Share it with all 40 new starters straight away and wait to see whether anyone reports a problem with an answer.
Include tricky cases in the test, such as a question the documents don't answer and an off-topic request.
Add several more rules covering situations she imagines might come up before running any tests at all.

questions.explanation: Instructions are only as good as the behavior they produce. Testing with **realistic questions whose answers she knows** shows whether Claude follows the format and uses the right sources. Adding **edge cases**, especially a question the documents don't cover and an out-of-scope request, checks the rules most likely to fail: the missing-information fallback and the scope boundary. Anthropic's testing guidance recommends mirroring the real distribution of requests and deliberately including edge cases such as irrelevant or missing input.

whyWrong.A: Claude's opinion that instructions 'look clear' is not evidence of how it will actually behave on real questions. Only testing shows that.
whyWrong.C: Using new hires as the test means wrong answers reach real people first, and many won't know an answer is wrong enough to report it.
whyWrong.E: Adding speculative rules before testing makes the instructions longer and harder to diagnose. Test first, then add rules only where behavior falls short.

questions.mindset: Check instructions by testing known answers and edge cases before real users depend on them.

questions.stem: An IT service desk lead built a Project to help staff with password resets, VPN access and laptop issues, using uploaded IT guides. Staff have started asking it payroll and holiday-allowance questions, and Claude answers confidently from general knowledge, sometimes contradicting HR policy. The lead wants to keep the project focused without frustrating staff. What is the BEST change to the instructions?

options.text: Define the scope in the instructions — IT support only — and tell Claude to redirect payroll and other questions to the HR portal.
Upload the HR handbook and payroll guides too, so the project can answer every kind of question staff might ask.
Add 'Refuse any question that is not about IT' with no further explanation, so staff learn to stop asking.
Rename the project 'IT ONLY – NO HR QUESTIONS' and add the same warning to the project description.

questions.explanation: Good system-level instructions define **scope** and say what to do with requests outside it. A short redirect to the right channel (the HR portal) keeps the project focused, stops answers from general knowledge that conflict with company policy, and still helps the person asking.

whyWrong.B: Turning an IT helper into an HR helper widens its purpose and ownership without HR's involvement. The IT lead would then be maintaining HR content nobody asked them to own.
whyWrong.C: A bare refusal stops the bad answers but leaves staff stuck with no idea where to go. It is unhelpful without a redirect.
whyWrong.D: A project's name and description help people find it; they are not instructions to Claude, so Claude's behavior would not change.

questions.mindset: Define the scope and give Claude a helpful redirect for anything outside it.

questions.stem: A finance business partner has a detailed, repeatable procedure for writing monthly variance commentary: a fixed structure, rules for rounding and wording, and a checklist. She needs it in several unrelated Projects and occasionally in ordinary chats, but most of her chats have nothing to do with variance reports. Where should this procedure live so it is applied when relevant WITHOUT cluttering every conversation?

options.text: In her account-wide instructions, so that it is available to every single conversation she has with Claude.
Copied into the instructions of each Project that uses it, and pasted into ordinary chats whenever she needs it.
In Claude's memory, by describing the procedure in a chat once and trusting Claude to remember it later.
Packaged as a Skill, available across her work, which Claude loads only when a task calls for it.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's help center contrasts always-on configuration with **Skills**: specialized procedures that are available to Claude but load dynamically when the task calls for them, rather than sitting in every prompt. A repeatable procedure that is needed in many places, but only some of the time, is exactly what a Skill is for.

whyWrong.A: Account-wide instructions apply to every chat, so a long reporting procedure would sit in conversations that have nothing to do with variance reports.
whyWrong.B: Copying the same procedure into several Projects and pasting it into chats creates multiple copies to keep in sync. One will eventually drift out of date.
whyWrong.C: Memory is what Claude picks up from past chats, not a reliable way to enforce a detailed procedure. Rules that must be followed should be written down where they are loaded deterministically.

questions.mindset: Match the layer to the reach: always-true preferences account-wide, one body of work in a Project, repeatable on-demand procedures in a Skill.
